subtype: Approach: talking to people who do the work [Action]
passage: Dear Vishal Bhaiya, thank you for spending Sunday's call telling your little cousin what a chartered accountant actually does all day. I've now asked three people: you, the architect whose office is near the bus stand, and our neighbour who is a nurse. In my notebook I wrote what each said was boring or stressful. You: matching bills line by line, and March deadlines. The architect: site visits in the heat, and clients who change their minds after the drawing is done. The nurse: standing for hours and night shifts, but she said one thank-you from a patient makes up for a lot. Reading the notes, I noticed the boring parts scare me less than the changing-minds part. I'll ask more questions before choosing anything. Love, Salma

qa.q: Which people did Salma ask about their day, besides the cousin?
qa.a: The architect near the bus stand and the nurse neighbour.

qa.q: What might Salma be feeling on rereading the notes?
qa.a: Thoughtful and slightly uneasy: the boring parts scare Salma less than clients who change their minds, so Salma wants to ask more before choosing.

qa.q: What else could Salma do to test her interest, and why?
qa.a: Spend a day observing or helping at one workplace, since a short tryout shows whether a real working day suits Salma better than descriptions do.

qa.q: How might the nurse neighbour see Salma's questions?
qa.a: The nurse is asked about a real day and not just the job title, so they may value the honest interest and feel free to describe the hard parts as well.

grounding: A student asks a cousin, an architect and a nurse neighbour about a normal day and records the boring and stressful parts.

subtype: Approach: small tryouts and measuring enjoyment [Action]
passage: Over two months in Accra, Abena tried three things and kept a small notebook of scores. First a coding tutorial on evenings after school. Then a weekend sketching project with a neighbour who painted signs. Then Saturday mornings at the clinic help desk, where Kofi, the volunteer coordinator, showed her how to greet people and point them to the right queue. After each one she wrote two numbers from one to five: energy and interest. Coding: 2 and 3. Sketching: 4 and 5. Clinic desk: 3 and 4. She noticed she picked up her sketchbook without being asked, and looked forward to Saturdays at the desk. She circled sketching, wrote “keep clinic Saturdays one more term,” and closed the notebook.

qa.q: What did Abena write down after each tryout?
qa.a: Two numbers from one to five: energy and interest.

qa.q: What did Abena's coding scores suggest about how she felt about it?
qa.a: Low energy and only middling interest: it felt tiring rather than exciting.

qa.q: What else could Abena do before choosing a path, and why?
qa.a: Talk to someone who works in the field she circled, because a tryout shows enjoyment but the daily reality of a job may differ.

qa.q: How might Kofi see Abena's ratings?
qa.a: Kofi sees volunteers come and go, so an honest weighing of the desk may be more useful than a student staying out of politeness.

grounding: A student tries coding, sketching and clinic volunteering over two months and rates energy and interest after each.

subtype: Approach: negotiating a win-win with parents [Action]
passage: On Saturday night Nilesh laid a printed sheet on the table: fees for both colleges, entrance dates in April, average job outcomes for each path. “Ma, Papa, I'll appear for the engineering exam. In the evenings I'll also build a design portfolio, six pieces by December. If my rank is good and the portfolio is weak, I choose engineering. If it's the other way round, we sit down and talk again.” His mother, Nirmala, pushed her glasses up and read the sheet twice. “You're not just saying you don't want engineering?” “No, Ma. I'm giving both a fair chance.” Papa asked how he would learn design. “A free online course to begin with.” Papa nodded slowly. “Six pieces by December. We'll look at them together.”

qa.q: By when does Nilesh plan to have six design pieces?
qa.a: By December.

qa.q: What might Nilesh be worried about while presenting the sheet?
qa.a: That his parents will hear it as a rejection of engineering, so he shows that both paths get a fair chance.

qa.q: What else could Nilesh do to strengthen the deal, and why?
qa.a: Ask a working designer and an engineer to comment on his plan and portfolio, because outside views help his parents trust the arrangement.

qa.q: How does the proposal look to Nirmala?
qa.a: Nirmala sees facts and a deadline, and that her son's idea keeps engineering open, so she may feel reassured that he is not simply refusing.

grounding: A student prepares facts and proposes a plan that honours both his parents' view and his own interest.

subtype: Approach: working backward from a desired lifestyle [Thinking]
passage: Dear Lakshmi Masi, you asked me what an ordinary Tuesday should look like in ten years, so I tried it. I want to wake up in a city of medium size like Nagpur, within a bus ride of Mummy and Papa, and sometimes work from home. Then I worked backwards: which jobs make that likely? Teaching, accounts in a local firm, software services with a nearby office. And which push it far away? Jobs that post you anywhere in the country, or firms in big cities with twelve-hour days. I've made a chart: field, qualification, cities where the work exists. Software and accounts look promising, and I can ask your friend at the software firm what it is really like. I'd been asking what to be. Now I'm asking how to live. — Vikas

qa.q: What kind of city does Vikas picture living in?
qa.a: A mid-sized city near family, where work can sometimes be done from home.

qa.q: What is Vikas feeling as the ordinary Tuesday takes shape on paper?
qa.a: Hopeful and clearer in mind: the picture of living near family with flexible hours gives the choice a direction.

qa.q: What else could Vikas do to check the chart, and why?
qa.a: Talk to someone who already lives that kind of life, because a real person can say whether flexible hours and local jobs actually exist.

qa.q: How might Lakshmi Masi see the letter?
qa.a: Lakshmi Masi, who asked the question, sees Vikas thinking about a way of life before job titles, and may be glad and offer to connect Vikas with the friend at the software firm.

grounding: A teen pictures a desired lifestyle and works backward to fields and qualifications that make it realistic.

subtype: Approach: following family expectation without examining it [Pitfall]
passage:
Rajni pulled a crumpled paper from her son's bag and smoothed it on the kitchen table.
“Twenty-one out of fifty?”
“Give it back.” Eshaan didn't look up. “Don't tell Papa. I'll fix it.”
“You used to draw until midnight. Now you say nothing at all. Eshaan, do you even like physics?”
“It doesn't matter. Papa and Bhaiya are engineers. That's the plan.”
“Who asked you if you wanted it?”
“Nobody had to.” He rubbed the edge of the table. “I sit in class and my head is somewhere else. I hid the last two tests as well.”
Rajni sat down slowly. “Two tests. And I only noticed today.”
He finally glanced up. “Are you angry?”
“No. I'm wondering why none of us asked.”

qa.q: What score did Eshaan get on the physics unit test?
qa.a: Twenty-one out of fifty.

qa.q: What might Eshaan be feeling as he says nobody had to ask?
qa.a: Resigned and ashamed: he hid his marks and assumed the family's plan left no room for what he wanted.

qa.q: What could Eshaan try instead, and why?
qa.a: He could talk honestly with his mother or a school counsellor about what interests him and what other streams offer, because choosing without asking whether he likes it is why he is bored and hiding marks.

qa.q: How does the situation look to Rajni?
qa.a: Rajni sees her son hiding marks and going quiet, and realises the family assumed his path without asking him, so she may feel worried and a little guilty.

grounding: A student picks the science stream because his father and elder brother are engineers, never asks himself whether he likes it, and hides poor marks.

subtype: Approach: copying a famous role model's path [Pitfall]
passage: The video ended at one in the morning, and Nandini was wide awake. A self-taught founder, no college, a company by twenty. “Why waste years on Class 11 and 12?” she told her cousin Yogesh the next day. “I'll learn everything myself.” Yogesh said, “Didn't he say his savings covered two years, an uncle gave him a room, and he'd been coding since he was twelve?” “That's just background.” She stopped preparing for the pre-boards and spent evenings watching more founder interviews. By March she had a notebook of app ideas, no working app, and a maths score that slid from seventy-two to fifty-five. Yogesh watched her scroll through another interview and said nothing this time.

qa.q: What did Yogesh remind Nandini about the founder?
qa.a: That his savings covered two years, an uncle gave him a room and he had been coding since he was twelve.

qa.q: What might Nandini be feeling when she asks why waste years on school?
qa.a: Impatient and inspired: the video made another few years of classes feel like a waste.

qa.q: What could Nandini do instead of copying the founder, and why?
qa.a: She could build a small project alongside school, since it tests her interest and skill without giving up her options.

qa.q: How does Nandini's plan look to Yogesh?
qa.a: Yogesh sees the parts of the story she left out, and worries she is copying the ending without the money, contacts and years of practice that made it possible.

grounding: A teen copies a famous founder's path and skips study, overlooking the savings, contacts and practice the founder had.

subtype: Approach: endless career quizzes and comparisons [Pitfall]
passage: “Bhupen, you asked why my stream form was empty at the deadline, so here's the embarrassing truth. I'm Vijay, and over six weeks I took twelve online aptitude tests. The first said I'm a natural artist, the second said lawyer, the third said I'd make an excellent pilot. Then I read forty lists, top jobs of the future, top jobs for introverts, top jobs by salary, and every list disagreed. The night before the form was due I had seventeen tabs open and a headache, and still no answer. I didn't lie awake deciding; I just stared. The next morning the class teacher gave me one extra day, and I had spent six weeks gathering results instead of asking a single person who does the work.”

qa.q: How many aptitude tests did Vijay take?
qa.a: Twelve.

qa.q: How did Vijay feel with seventeen tabs open the night before the deadline?
qa.a: Overwhelmed and stuck: the conflicting results left no clear answer.

qa.q: What could Vijay have done instead of taking more quizzes, and why?
qa.a: Pick two or three fields and speak with people who work in them or try a small tryout, since real information cuts through conflicting quiz results.

qa.q: How might the class teacher see Vijay's empty form?
qa.a: The class teacher sees a form still blank at the deadline and, having given an extra day, may worry that Vijay has no plan and want to sit down and talk.

grounding: A student takes a dozen quizzes and reads forty lists, gets conflicting results, and reaches the deadline with no decision.

subtype: Approach: revisiting the choice after weak feedback [Revision]
passage: In the counselling room, Afreen laid her chemistry paper on the table: twenty-eight out of a hundred, the third low score this term. “I study every night,” she said. “Effort isn't the problem.” Zainab ma'am, the school counsellor, nodded and asked, “Which subjects make you forget the time?” “Maths. Statistics puzzles.” Afreen paused. “I've been avoiding that, because everyone says medicine is the real thing.” She rubbed her eyes. “Maybe medicine isn't for me.” Zainab ma'am didn't argue; she only asked, “What would you like to do about it?” Afreen took a pen and wrote data and statistics at the top of a new page, and beneath it: ask for the maths elective, talk to Papa on Sunday. Her voice was shaky, but her shoulders looked lighter.

qa.q: What score did Afreen get on the chemistry paper?
qa.a: Twenty-eight out of a hundred.

qa.q: What was Afreen feeling as she said maybe medicine isn't for me?
qa.a: Sad but relieved: her voice was shaky, yet her shoulders looked lighter.

qa.q: What could Afreen do to test the new path, and why?
qa.a: She could try a short statistics course or small project first, since a small tryout shows whether the path suits her before she commits.

qa.q: How might Papa see the change?
qa.a: Papa may be surprised and worried because medicine was the plan, so Afreen's talk on Sunday, with her marks and an idea for the elective, could help him understand.

grounding: After weak chemistry marks despite effort, a student meets a counsellor, admits medicine may not fit and moves toward data and statistics.

subtype: Approach: keeping the choice reversible for now [Revision]
passage: The stream form was due by four that afternoon, and the corridor buzzed with students queuing at the staffroom. Leela stood in line, pen wobbling. Science or commerce? She still didn't know. “Take the one that closes fewer doors,” she muttered, and ticked science. Wasim Sir, the class teacher, was juggling twenty forms, but Leela stopped him. “Sir, can we write a review date? After the first term.” He blinked, then took out a pen. On the back of the form they wrote: review the week after first-term exams; change if two tests in a row fall below fifty in maths and physics, or if lab days feel like dread. Leela signed under it, feeling that the tick was not a lock.

qa.q: When will Leela's choice be reviewed?
qa.a: The week after the first-term exams.

qa.q: What might Leela be feeling as she signs under the review note?
qa.a: Uncertain but relieved: she still does not know, but the review date means the tick is not final.

qa.q: What else could Leela do during the term to inform the review, and why?
qa.a: Sit in on a commerce class or talk to older students who switched, because first-hand views show what the other stream is really like.

qa.q: How does the arrangement look to Wasim Sir?
qa.a: Wasim Sir, busy with twenty forms, gets a clear rule for when to revisit, so he can support Leela without pushing her either way.

grounding: Unsure between streams, a teen picks the one that keeps more doors open and agrees a review date and change triggers with teachers.

subtype: Approach: working backward from the exam date [Thinking]
passage: Vikas stood in front of the wall calendar and counted: nineteen weeks to the entrance test. On an index card went the syllabus, twenty-four units. Then the subtracting began. The last three weeks would be revision only. Four weeks in the middle would go to full mock papers. That left twelve weeks for twenty-four units, so two units a week, no more, no less. Vikas wrote 2/week in red and pinned the card above the desk. Darshan, who studied at the next desk, leaned over. “And if a week goes wrong?” “Then it eats into the mock weeks, and I move things.” Vikas breathed out. A large, blurry number had become a small list.

qa.q: How many units must Vikas finish each week?
qa.a: Two units a week.

qa.q: What might Vikas be feeling after the calculation?
qa.a: Relief and steadiness: the big blurry number became a small list 🙂.

qa.q: What else could Vikas add to the plan, and why?
qa.a: A spare week for illness or slow topics, since a buffer keeps one bad week from breaking the whole plan.

qa.q: How does the plan look to Darshan?
qa.a: Darshan, studying at the next desk, sees a vague worry turned into a schedule, and may want a plan like it or worry about one bad week.

grounding: A student counts the weeks before the exam, lists the units and works backward to a weekly number including revision and mocks.
